source.title: The True Prosoluble Completion of a Group: Examples and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: Profinite Grothendieck problem for groups: let Gamma and Delta be residually finite groups, and let psi: Gamma -> Delta be a homomorphism such that the induced map on profinite completions PF(psi): PF(Gamma) -> PF(Delta) is an isomorphism, where PF(G) is the completion of G with respect to all finite-index normal subgroups. How far can psi fail to be an isomorphism? In particular, beyond the known examples where psi is not an isomorphism, what structural or finiteness hypotheses on Gamma and Delta force psi itself to be an isomorphism?

evidence.quote: (i) Let Γ, ∆ be two residually finite groups and let ψ : Γ −→ ∆ be a homomorphism such that, at the profinite level, the corresponding homomorphism P F (ψ) : P F (Γ) −→ P F (∆) is an isomorphism. How far from an isomorphism can ψ be?

There are examples with ψ not an isomorphism and P F (ψ) an isomorphism, with Γ, ∆ finitely generated [PlaTa–86] and finitely presented [BriGr–04]. If P F (ψ) is an isomorphism, there are known sufficient conditions1 on Γ and ∆ for ψ to be an isomorphism.

accepted.question_text: Prosoluble analogue of Grothendieck's problem: let Gamma and Delta be residually soluble groups, and let psi: Gamma -> Delta be a homomorphism such that the induced map on true prosoluble completions PS(psi): PS(Gamma) -> PS(Delta) is an isomorphism, where PS(G) is the completion of G with respect to all normal subgroups N for which G/N is soluble. How far can psi fail to be an isomorphism? In particular, which additional hypotheses on Gamma and Delta, such as finite generation or finite presentation, are sufficient to force psi itself to be an isomorphism?

evidence.quote: Our main interest in this paper is the prosoluble analogue of Grothendieck’s problem. More precisely, let again Γ, ∆ be two groups and ψ : Γ −→ ∆ a homomorphism, but assume now that the groups are residually soluble. Assume that, at the true prosoluble level, the corresponding homomorphism P S(ψ) : P S(Γ) −→ P S(∆) is an isomorphism. How far from an isomorphism can ψ be? Additional requirements can be added on Γ and ∆ (such as finite generation, finite presentation, ...).

accepted.question_text: Let G be a complete Hausdorff topological group such that every nonidentity element g in G is omitted by some open normal subgroup N of G with soluble quotient G/N. Find useful characterizations of when such a topological group G is isomorphic to the true prosoluble completion PS(Gamma) of a residually soluble discrete group Gamma. In particular, how can one decide whether G is isomorphic to PS(Gamma) for some finitely generated Gamma, and how can one decide whether G is isomorphic to PS(Gamma) for some finitely presented Gamma?

evidence.quote: (iii) Can one find interesting characterizations of those groups which are true prosoluble completions of residually soluble group? More precisely, let G be a complete Hausdorff topological group such that, for any g ∈ G, g 6= 1, there exists an open normal subgroup N of G not containing g such that G/N is soluble; how can it be decided whether G is isomorphic to P S(Γ) for some finitely generated group Γ? for some finitely presented group Γ?

accepted.question_text: Let Gamma be the first Grigorchuk group, identified with its image in its profinite completion PF(Gamma), which also coincides in this setting with its pro-2 completion, true prosoluble completion, and usual prosoluble completion. Does there exist an element g in PF(Gamma) \ Gamma such that the subgroup Delta generated by Gamma and g inside PF(Gamma) has the congruence subgroup property, meaning that every normal subgroup N of Delta is of the form M intersect Delta for some open normal subgroup M of PF(Gamma)? Producing such an element would give a new example of a non-isomorphic homomorphism psi: Gamma -> Delta whose induced map on profinite completions PF(psi) is an isomorphism.

evidence.quote: (4.G) Say that a subgroup ∆ of a profinite group G has the congruence subgroup property if any normal subgroup N of ∆ is of the form N = M ∩ ∆ for some open normal subgroup M of G.

(4.H) Let G be a finitely generated profinite group, and ∆ a dense subgroup of G. Let ψ : ∆ −→ G denote the inclusion. As in (4.G), the corresponding continuous homomorphism P F (∆) −→ G is always onto, and it is an isomorphism if and only if ∆ has the congruence subgroup property.
Open problem. Let Γ be the first Grigorchuk group; it is an infinite group which is residually a finite 2–group, and all its proper quotients are finite 2–groups.
The problem is to find an element g in the complement of Γ in P F (Γ) such that the subgroup ∆ of P F (Γ) generated by Γ and g has the congruence subgroup property.
This would provide one more example of a homomorphism ψ : Γ −→ ∆ which is not an isomorphism and which would be such that the homomorphism P F (ψ) is an isomorphism,
namely one solution to the original Grothendieck problem of a different nature than the existing ones (from [PlaTa–86], [PlaTa–89], and [BriGr–04]).

accepted.question_text: For an abstract group Gamma that is not residually soluble, what can be said about the true prosoluble kernel Ker(Gamma -> PS(Gamma))? Equivalently, determine the intersection over n >= 0 of D_n(Gamma), where D_0(Gamma)=Gamma and D_{n+1}(Gamma)=[D_n(Gamma),D_n(Gamma)] is the ordinary derived series. In particular, investigate this kernel for non-residually-soluble one-relator groups, wreath products as in the paper, free products of nilpotent groups with amalgamation, parafree groups, and meta-residually soluble groups, including free-by-free groups that are not residually soluble.

Examples to investigate include: other one–relator groups which are not residually soluble; wreath products as in (6.B); free products of nilpotent groups with amalgamation (see for example Proposition 7 in [Kahro1]); parafree groups (see (7.B)); meta–residually soluble groups, namely groups having a residually soluble normal subgroup with residually soluble quotient (see Theorem 2 in [Kahro2]); particular cases: free–by–free groups which are not residually soluble.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a discrete group Gamma such that Gamma is residually finite and residually soluble, so the canonical homomorphisms Gamma -> PF(Gamma) and Gamma -> PS(Gamma) are injective, but the canonical homomorphism Gamma -> PFS(Gamma) is not injective, where PFS(Gamma) is the completion with respect to normal subgroups whose quotients are finite and soluble?

evidence.quote: (6.G) Does there exist a discrete group Γ which on the one hand is residually finite and residually soluble, namely for which both homomorphisms Γ −→ P F (Γ), Γ −→ P S(Γ) are injective, and which on the other hand is such that the homomorphism Γ −→ P F S(Γ) is NOT injective?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a finitely generated free group F, a residually soluble group Gamma that is not free, and a homomorphism psi: F -> Gamma such that for every j >= 1 the induced homomorphism F/D_j(F) -> Gamma/D_j(Gamma) is an isomorphism, where D_j denotes the j-th term of the ordinary derived series? Equivalently, does there exist such F, Gamma, and psi for which the induced map on true prosoluble completions PS(psi): PS(F) -> PS(Gamma) is an isomorphism?
accepted.context_brief: Free versus nonfree true prosoluble completions

evidence.quote: We do not know if there exist a finitely generated free group F, a group Γ which is residually soluble and not free, and a homomorphism ψ : F −→ Γ such that ψ induces an isomorphism F/Dj (F ) −→ Γ/Dj (Γ) for all j ≥ 1, or equivalently such that P S(ψ) : P S(F ) −→ P S(Γ) is an isomorphism.

trace.notes: Normalized the input as the zbMATH resolver URL https://zbmath.org/5180049. Local shard metadata identified the exact work as 'The true prosoluble completion of a group: examples and open problems.' with DOI 10.1007/s10711-006-9103-y and arXiv identifier math/0512242.

Direct shell network fetches for zbmath.org, api.zbmath.org, and Zenodo failed with DNS resolution errors in this environment. The already cached local PDF .sisyphus/paper-question-parser/tmp/math-0512242.pdf was used as the readable exact-work artifact; its first page visibly gives arXiv:math/0512242v2 and the title 'THE TRUE PROSOLUBLE COMPLETION OF A GROUP EXAMPLES AND OPEN PROBLEMS'.

Mapped the PDF. Section hierarchy: 1. Introduction; 2. Completion with respect to a directed set of normal subgroups; 3. Universal property; 4. Examples of directed sets of normal subgroups; 5. True prosoluble completions; 6. Examples; 7. On the true prosoluble and the true pronilpotent analogues of Grothendieck's problem; References. Key notation includes PF(Gamma) for profinite completion, PS(Gamma) for true prosoluble completion, PFS(Gamma) for finite-soluble procompletion, and D_n(Gamma) for derived-series terms. Likely open-problem regions are page 2, pages 7-8, page 11, and page 13.

The introduction contains explicit open questions for the profinite Grothendieck problem, its true prosoluble analogue, and characterization of topological groups that arise as true prosoluble completions.
Sections 2 and 3 define completion machinery and universal properties but do not introduce a distinct open problem.
Section 4 contains the explicit Grigorchuk-group open problem in subsection 4.H, using the congruence subgroup property defined in subsection 4.G.
Section 5 supplies definitions and identifications for true prosoluble completions and derived-series quotients but does not add a separate candidate.

Section 6 contains one broad investigation problem about the true prosoluble kernel for non-residually-soluble groups and one explicit existence question about a group with injective maps to PF and PS but noninjective map to PFS.

Section 7 contains one unresolved existence problem in subsection 7.C concerning a free group, a nonfree residually soluble group, and isomorphisms on all derived-series quotients. Subsection 7.B gives related pronilpotent context but no additional distinct open question from this source.

Expanded the profinite Grothendieck problem into a standalone formulation by defining PF as completion with respect to finite-index normal subgroups and by preserving the paper's question about how far psi can be from an isomorphism.

Expanded the prosoluble analogue by defining PS through normal subgroups with soluble quotient and making the finite-generation and finite-presentation hypotheses explicit as possible added assumptions.
Made the topological separation condition self-contained and separated the finitely generated and finitely presented decision questions.
Rewrote the Grigorchuk-group problem as a self-contained existence question, including the relevant completion coincidences and the stated Grothendieck-problem consequence.

Converted the programmatic kernel problem into a standalone question by spelling out Ker(Gamma -> PS(Gamma)) as the intersection of derived-series terms and listing the example families named in the source.
Restated the existence question by distinguishing residual finiteness, residual solubility, and noninjectivity into PFS(Gamma), the completion over finite soluble quotients.
Inlined the derived-series quotient condition and the equivalent true-prosoluble-completion formulation from subsection 7.C.

No candidates were merged. The profinite problem, prosoluble analogue, characterization problem, Grigorchuk specialization, kernel problem, PFS-injectivity problem, and free-versus-nonfree derived-series problem have different hypotheses and targets.

All accepted items passed self-containedness, evidence coverage, evidence completeness, no-new-facts, source adequacy, and schema conformance checks. Each accepted item includes solved-status metadata and at least one page-numbered evidence quote from the readable PDF artifact.
